entries.title: Storms push Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City to Saturday
entries.summary: The parade, which marks its 100th edition, got a last-minute rain check ahead of heavy gusts on Thursday.
entries.content:
The parade, which marks its 100th edition, got a last-minute rain check ahead of heavy gusts on Thursday.

New York City is famous for its annual Thanksgiving Day Parade, a procession of towering helium balloons, elaborate floats and marching bands.

But on Wednesday, organisers in the United States announced that this year’s edition has been postponed because of an East Coast storm that threatens turbulent weather.

It was rescheduled for Saturday instead, right after Black Friday, a day when retailers traditionally offer holiday shopping and discount prices.

The annual parade is sponsored by Macy’s, a New York-based department store brand, and Saturday’s event will be its 100th Thanksgiving procession.

“While we are heartbroken that our parade was postponed, the safety of our participants and spectators is and always will be our top priority,” Will Coss, Macy’s executive producer, said in a Wednesday news conference.

“ We’re saddened by the shift, but we’re optimistic about our opportunity to deliver the most spectacular 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, the best and biggest parade in our history.”

The parade, founded in 1924, was cancelled three times during World War II, but this year marks the first time it was postponed.

The event’s signature balloons were already being inflated on Wednesday when Macy’s announced the delay.

The decision came amid warnings issued by the National Weather Service of lashing winds and possible coastal flooding for the New York City area.

Gusts are forecast to reach up to 97 km/h, and rainfall of 2.5 to 5cm is expected from Thursday into Friday. A high wind warning is also in effect from 10am local time (15:00 GMT) Thursday through 1am (6:00 GMT) Friday.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani described the decision as tough but necessary given the forecast.

“I know that this change of plans will cause inconveniences. Yet safety has to come first,” he said at Wednesday’s news conference. “On Saturday, when balloons climb into the sky, every New Yorker and everyone visiting will be able to take in a show that is both truly spectacular and also safe.”

The holiday extravaganza typically draws more than 3.5 million spectators along its Manhattan route, according to New York City authorities. It is also broadcast nationwide.

For many Americans, the parade is a fixture of Thanksgiving, and the postponement marks a break with a familiar holiday ritual.

NBC, the television network that airs the annual parade, said it would instead broadcast a repeat of the 2025 edition on Thursday.

It remains unclear whether the full roster of performers scheduled for the parade will continue to perform on Saturday. According to Macy’s website, singers like Raye and Wyclef Jean were scheduled to headline, as were actors and Broadway stars like Leslie Odom Jr and Anthony Ramos.

New floats include a five-storey-tall balloon of the cartoon character Bluey wearing a crown, and a 17-meter-long version of the beagle Snoopy carrying his bird sidekick Woodstock.

There will also be a blue hippopotamus, a nod to the balloon that floated off from the 1931 parade and was lost.

Mamdani assured New Yorkers that the parade route would be safe once the storm passes on Saturday, thanks to a surge of law enforcement.

“ There will be an expanded police presence this Saturday along the route, and the [New York Police Department] is fully prepared for an event of this magnitude, just as they have been prepared for the 99 parades that preceded this,” Mamdani said.

“I want to make clear that there are no known specific or credible threats to the parade at this time.”

The festivities are slated to begin at 8:30am local time (13:30 GMT).

entries.title: ISIL blamed for multiple suicide attacks in Syria
entries.summary: ISIL suicide attack kills two in an assault on a security post in northeastern Syria.
entries.content:
ISIL blamed for multiple suicide attacks in Syria

NewsFeed

ISIL blamed for multiple suicide attacks in Syria

Two members of Syria’s security forces have been killed in a suicide attack on a security post in Hasakah, in north-eastern Syria. Five others were injured. Authorities accuse ISIL for sending four attackers who used suicide vests and a motorcycle laden with explosives.

Published On 26 Nov 2026

entries.title: Two Syrian security personnel killed in ISIL suicide attack
entries.summary: Syrian forces say the attack in northeastern Syria's city of Hasakah involved four assailants who were all killed.
entries.content:
Syrian forces say the attack in northeastern Syria’s city of Hasakah involved four assailants who were all killed.

A suicide attack by the ISIL (ISIS) group has killed two security personnel and wounded five others in Syria’s northeastern city of Hasakah, according to local authorities.

Four gunmen targeted an Internal Security Forces (ISF) checkpoint on Wednesday in the Mushirfa neighbourhood of Hasakah, an official statement from the governorate’s media directorate said.

All four of the assailants died in the attack, two in clashes with security forces and the other two in suicide explosions, the ISF said.

One of the suicide attackers, Syrian media reported, was riding a booby-trapped motorcycle when he detonated himself at the entrance of the post.

The deputy governor of Hasakah, Ahmed al-Hilali, vowed “to uncover the circumstances of the attack and identify the perpetrators”.

“Ensuring the safety of citizens and the stability of the region is a responsibility from which we will not waver,” al-Hilali added.

The ISF shared photos from the site on their X page, including an image of the vest they say was worn by one of the two perpetrators who was “neutralised” by the forces.

Continued attacks

A report in February by the UN said that Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa and two of his senior cabinet ministers were the targets of five foiled assassination attempts by ISIL over the past year.

The report did not provide specific dates as to when the foiled attacks took place, though it noted their locations in northern Aleppo, the country’s most populous province, and the southern province of Deraa.

In October, the Interior Ministry reported that two members of Syria’s internal security forces were killed and five wounded in clashes with a suspected ISIL cell during a raid on the outskirts of Damascus.

entries.title: Zambia bans protest against push to remove presidential term limits
entries.summary: Critics fear the campaign could undermine democratic safeguards as senior opposition figures remain behind bars.
entries.content:
Critics fear the campaign could undermine democratic safeguards as senior opposition figures remain behind bars.

Lusaka, Zambia – Zambian authorities have banned a planned protest against calls to remove presidential term limits, amid mounting concerns over political freedoms following President Hakainde Hichilema’s disputed re-election in August.

The demonstration, scheduled for November 25, was organised by civil society groups and human rights defenders opposed to proposals that could allow Hichilema to remain in power beyond 2031, when his second and final five-year term is due to end.

Police cited the risk of clashes after a pro-government youth group announced plans to hold a rival demonstration in support of removing presidential term limits.

Three organisations aligned with the governing United Party for National Development (UPND) have petitioned the National Assembly to remove constitutional restrictions on presidential terms, potentially paving the way for Hichilema to seek a third term.

The campaign has drawn opposition from civil society organisations, the influential Catholic Church and the Law Association of Zambia (LAZ), which have called for an end to the debate over extending presidential tenure.

Hichilema, who swept to power in 2021 on a promise of democratic reforms, had repeatedly criticised African leaders who sought to extend their rule through constitutional amendments.

His office has sought to reassure critics. In a statement on November 20, presidential communications official Clayson Hamasaka said Hichilema would respect the constitution “at all times”.

“The president also respects every citizen’s right to freedom of expression,” Hamasaka said.

But the campaign to remove term limits, coupled with the prolonged detention of senior opposition figures, has raised concerns among government critics about the future of one of Africa’s more established multiparty democracies.

‘We are being blocked from protesting’

On November 4, civil society organisations and human rights defenders notified police of their intention to march against the removal of presidential term limits.

A pro-government youth alliance subsequently announced plans to demonstrate in support of the proposals, prompting police to cite the risk of confrontations between the two groups.

Minister of Home Affairs and Internal Security Clement Andeleki defended the decision to cancel the demonstrations, dismissing suggestions that Hichilema was seeking a third term.

“We cancelled [the protests] because those are trying to go to the streets, they are going to do what? Because there is no third term that the president [Hichilema] wants,” Andeleki told Al Jazeera.

The decision came days after Justice Minister Jack Mwiimbu pledged to protect citizens exercising their right to petition parliament for the removal of presidential term limits.

“We’ll not allow individuals threatening others who are exercising their rights to express themselves freely,” Mwiimbu told journalists in Lusaka on November 18, adding that Hichilema would respect any amendments to the constitution.

Linda Kasonde, a former president of the Law Association of Zambia and one of the organisers of the planned demonstration, said the group had appealed against the police decision.

“We have seen that we are being blocked from protesting and so, we have written to the police to give us an alternative date and we have also written to the minister of home affairs to appeal the decision of police,” Kasonde told Al Jazeera.

She said the organisers remained committed to peaceful protest and wanted to demonstrate public opposition to the removal of presidential term limits.

A disputed election and opposition crackdown

The controversy comes against the backdrop of a disputed general election and the detention of some of Hichilema’s most prominent political opponents.

Hichilema was re-elected in August with more than 61 percent of the vote in an election in which observers, including the European Union Election Observation Mission, reported irregularities.

A six-hour suspension of vote counting and the announcement of results, the deployment of soldiers at polling stations and tallying centres, and the removal of opposition and independent monitors raised questions about the credibility of the electoral process.

The closure of courts following the election also raised concerns over the opposition’s ability to challenge the results.

Brian Mundubile, who finished second in the presidential race and accused Hichilema of electoral fraud, was arrested alongside his running mate, Makebi Zulu, in a post-election crackdown.

Then, former minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was fatally wounded by security forces during a raid on a house in Lusaka where senior opposition figures were meeting.

Mundubile, Zulu and several other opposition figures have been detained for more than 100 days over allegations of attempting to overthrow Hichilema’s government and engaging in seditious activities.

The accused say the charges are politically motivated.

Their prolonged detention has drawn condemnation from local and international human rights defenders and prompted a legal challenge against the state.

A day before the High Court was due to rule on their continued detention, prosecutors produced a charge sheet alleging treason.

Sakwiba Sikota, a leading defence lawyer, told Al Jazeera that the trial was expected to begin in 2027.

Treason is a non-bailable offence in Zambia and carries a possible life sentence. Lengthy legal proceedings could keep some of the country’s most prominent opposition figures out of public life for monthsm or even years.

Muhabi Lungu, secretary-general of the Tonse Alliance, the opposition coalition led by Mundubile, alleged that the prosecutions were intended to weaken the opposition ahead of possible constitutional changes.

“This scheme was hatched a long time ago, and so, this treason issue is an attempt to try and denigrate the opposition so that somehow, they can justify why he must continue beyond the constitutional requirement,” Lungu told Al Jazeera.

He urged the authorities to expedite the trial and make public the evidence against the accused.

The battle over presidential term limits

Supporters of the proposed changes argue that presidential term limits restrict voters’ democratic right to choose their leaders.

Mark Simuuwe, the UPND’s head of media, rejected suggestions that the campaign was specifically intended to secure a third term for Hichilema.

“We are not talking about a third term bid here; instead we are talking about removal of the term limit restrictions because we feel the current constitution is undemocratic as it denies electorates a chance to elect a president of their choice when they want to,” Simuuwe said in an interview.

A constitutional amendment would require the support of at least two-thirds of parliamentarians, although additional constitutional procedures may apply to changes affecting presidential tenure.

The UPND does not command a two-thirds majority in the National Assembly but could seek support from independent legislators and other members of parliament.

For critics, however, removing presidential term limits would risk dismantling an important democratic safeguard in a country that has experienced several peaceful transfers of power since the introduction of multiparty democracy in 1991.

Among them was Hichilema’s own election victory in 2021, when he defeated incumbent President Edgar Lungu.

A wider regional trend

The debate in Zambia comes as constitutional changes elsewhere in Africa have renewed concerns over presidential tenure and democratic accountability.

In neighbouring Zimbabwe, President Emmerson Mnangagwa signed into law constitutional amendments in July that would allow him to remain in office two years beyond his previous term limit.

The amendments extend presidential terms from five to seven years and replace direct presidential elections with a system under which parliament selects the president.

In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, another of Zambia’s neighbours, President Felix Tshisekedi has approved legislation allowing constitutional changes to be put to a referendum, a development that critics fear could pave the way for a third presidential term.

In Zambia, the debate over term limits is unfolding as opposition leaders remain behind bars and civil society groups await a response from the authorities on whether they will be allowed to demonstrate.

For Kasonde, the campaign to remove term limits cannot be separated from the political tensions that followed the August election.

“This attempt to remove the term limits to consolidate power is not for ideological reasons but because of the [decline in] legitimacy following a controversial election,” she said.

entries.title: A meeting with Democrats over healthcare? Trump says he’s open to it
entries.summary: Experts tell Al Jazeera they are sceptical that Trump would back Medicare for All, a proposal for national healthcare.
entries.content:
Experts tell Al Jazeera they are sceptical that Trump would back Medicare for All, a proposal for national healthcare.

Just weeks after attacking Abdul El-Sayed on the campaign trail, United States President Donald Trump says he will meet with the incoming Democratic senator to discuss Medicare for All, a proposal to establish a national healthcare programme.

Trump confirmed his willingness to sit down with El-Sayed in an interview with the New York Post on Tuesday, calling the Democrat a “smart guy”.

“I know I’ll be meeting with him,” Trump said. “Maybe there’s some place in the middle that we could go.”

A former public health official in Detroit, El-Sayed catapulted to national prominence in the 2026 midterm elections, when he won a hotly contested Senate seat in Michigan. A central part of his platform has been expanding access to healthcare.

In an interview with Zeteo this month, El-Sayed even floated renaming Medicare for All after Trump.

“If he wants to pass Trumpcare for All, I’m OK with it,” El-Sayed told host Mehdi Hasan. “He seems to like to put his name on things.”

Days later, he posted on social media a mockup of a gold-colored insurance card, bearing Trump’s signature and the name “Trumpcare”.

In an accompanying caption, El-Sayed asked the president to “guarantee health care for every American, from cradle to grave”.

The White House initially dismissed the proposal. Then, on Saturday, Trump shared El-Sayed’s image of the card on Truth Social. In his interview with the New York Post, Trump also called the “Trumpcare” branding “very smart”.

El-Sayed is pitching a government-run health insurance programme, which would cover “all necessary healthcare” and still allow private insurance.

Trump has not endorsed the proposal, and there is no set date for the meeting.

But with Democrats set to take control of the US Congress in January, healthcare advocates and political experts are closely watching what will come out of any potential meeting between the two politicians.

It remains unclear what Trump’s support could mean for the effort to get guaranteed healthcare for every American.

A long road for US healthcare

For more than a century, the US has weighed the possibility of offering universal healthcare access. But such proposals in recent decades have faced stiff opposition from the private sector.

During the Great Depression in the 1930s, for instance, President Franklin D Roosevelt appointed a Committee on Economic Security whose mission was to address the need for “all forms of social insurance”, including healthcare.

While a national health bill did not pass during Roosevelt’s administration, his successor, Harry Truman, became the first US president to propose a comprehensive national health insurance system in 1945. It failed amid fierce opposition from the American Medical Association, which called it “socialized medicine”.

Twenty years later, President Lyndon B Johnson signed two government insurance programmes, Medicare and Medicaid, into law. But their scope was limited to providing coverage for older Americans and some people in low-income brackets or with special needs.

Since then, a number of Democratic leaders have tried different paths to expand coverage.

In 1994, President Bill Clinton’s plan proposed giving everyone healthcare through private insurance, with employers required to help pay for it. Insurers ran advertisements warning the plan would limit people’s medical choices, and the plan died without a vote amid divisions in the US Congress.

The next Democratic president, Barack Obama, took up the fight to expand healthcare access again in the new millennium.

His name became associated with a sweeping overhaul of the US healthcare system — the Affordable Care Act, popularly known as “Obamacare” — that passed in 2010.

The Affordable Care Act expanded Medicaid, helped people pay for private insurance and made it illegal for insurers to turn people away because of pre-existing conditions. But a proposal to let people buy a government-run plan alongside private options failed in the US Senate.

During the 2016 and 2020 presidential campaigns, Senator Bernie Sanders, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, made Medicare for All a centrepiece of his platform, proposing a federal plan to replace most private insurance, including the coverage people get through work.

While the idea was embraced by progressives, Democrats as a whole were divided over whether to replace private coverage and who would bear the cost.

Sanders and his allies introduced another bill in 2025, but it has yet to pass through the US Congress.

Eagan Kemp, a healthcare policy expert at the consumer advocacy nonprofit Public Citizen, believes such proposals have struggled because of the economic heft the healthcare industry wields.

“I think the big reason is profit,” said Eagan Kemp. He described the country’s medical system as the “Wild West”.

In the 1980s, US healthcare costs were similar to those in other countries, according to Kemp.

But the American system became more corporatised and driven by profit, he explained, and it lacked the regulation many countries introduced as they moved towards universal healthcare.

Kemp argued that programmes like Medicare for All would rein in what companies can charge, how much care they can cut and how much profit they can take out of the system.

It would also cut out the insurance middlemen that drive up costs and make it harder for people to get the care they need, he said.

Sceptical but hopeful

Experts note that Trump’s flirtation with El-Sayed’s Medicare for All proposal isn’t drawing the amount of opposition that would be expected for what has historically been a very partisan issue.

Republican strategist Ashley Davis, who worked in President George W Bush’s administration, told Al Jazeera she was bullish that Trump could pick up some bipartisan support on healthcare, an area she says he’s been “focused on”.

“I’m actually happy they’re meeting because, maybe for once, Republicans and Democrats can get along and something productive will come out of this,” Davis told Al Jazeera.

However, she expressed doubt that a bill resembling Medicare for All will materialise from any meeting with El-Sayed, saying agreements to lower drug prices, provide more funds for rural healthcare or expand Medicare for children are much more likely.

In order to pass something like Medicare for All, Davis explained that “you would have to bring on some of the new [Democratic] senators in really red states”.

“It sounds great from a talking point perspective, but how it actually gets accomplished is a whole other thing,” she added.

Kemp was also sceptical that a policy like Medicare for All could cruise through the US Congress to Trump’s desk, citing the high number of political donations that lawmakers receive from healthcare and insurance providers.

“How much they’d be willing to do, or how quickly they’d be willing to move, is yet to be determined,” he said of the country’s Congress members. “I’m sceptical that there would be votes there.”

But Kemp noted that Trump has a tendency to break from Republican orthodoxy. The fact that he is not competing on the ballot in 2028 could also help pave the way for healthcare discussions with Democrats.

It may also be the last chance for Trump, who has described himself as a world-class dealmaker, to get a major piece of legislation passed during his final two years in the White House, according to Kemp.

“If it was any other Republican president in my lifetime, I wouldn’t hold much hope,” he said. “But I think this one will be interesting to see play out.”

entries.title: Iran war live: Explosion rocks Sanaa; missiles intercepted over Riyadh
entries.summary: A blast hits Sanaa after air strikes near the airport, as the Saudi coalition intercepts missiles over Riyadh.
entries.content:
Live updatesLive updates,

Iran war live: Explosion rocks Sanaa; missiles intercepted over Riyadh

Published On 26 Nov 2026

  • An explosion rocks Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, following recent air strikes near its international airport, while the Saudi-led coalition says its air defences intercepted two ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis towards Riyadh.
  • A tanker’s master reports an explosion from an unknown projectile close to the vessel 50 nautical miles (93km) west of Dubai in the UAE, with no injuries or damage reported, UKMTO says.

entries.title: Houthis target Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea ports as strikes escalate
entries.summary: Explosion reported in Sanaa after Saudi air defenses intercept ballistic missiles targeting Riyadh.
entries.content:
Explosion reported in Sanaa after Saudi air defenses intercept ballistic missiles targeting Riyadh.

Yemen’s Houthi group has struck the port of Jizan on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea coast as fighting intensifies near the Yemeni city of Taiz.

A Saudi-led military coalition said a Houthi attack on Jizan caused only minor damage and no civilian casualties on Wednesday, adding that “efforts are underway to determine the type of projectile” used.

The spokesman for the coalition, Turki al-Maliki, later said in a statement on X that its forces intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone over Jeddah’s port in Saudi Arabia.

No civilian injuries were reported from falling debris following the interception, he added.

After the coalition’s statement, an explosion was heard in Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, according to Al Jazeera’s Nabil al-Yousfi.

The Saudi-led coalition then said its air defences intercepted and destroyed ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards Saudi Arabia’s capital, Riyadh.

The attempted strike on the capital follows a Houthi drone attack on a skyscraper in Riyadh’s financial district on Tuesday, injuring at least 11 people.

The latest incidents mark a further escalation between the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi Arabia, including strikes from both sides targeting airports, energy facilities and other civilian and economic infrastructure.

The strikes on Saudi Arabian ports come after the Houthi-affiliated Al Masirah TV reported new Saudi attacks on the port of Hodeidah in Yemen.

Earlier on Wednesday, the Houthis threatened to attack Saudi ports if Hodeidah came under attack.

“The port of Hodeidah handles 90 percent of imported goods into Yemen. If it is closed, it could bring the humanitarian situation to the brink of collapse”, said Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Yemen’s capital, Sanaa.

“Some of Saudi Arabia’s recent attacks at the Port of Hodeidah have targeted storage tanks and cranes used to load and unload shipments”, Mawry said.

Fighting in Yemen

Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces have been battling the Houthis on several fronts, with the army’s spokesman saying 654 strikes have been carried out against the group on Wednesday.

Yemen’s western front has witnessed the heaviest concentration of recent strikes, according to Al Jazeera’s Maha Ali, reporting from Taiz.

Government forces have said air strikes targeted Houthi positions west of Taiz.

“These strikes are part of an intense and sustained wave of air raids that have continued for approximately 72 hours”, Ali said.

“Particular attention is focused on the most significant mountain range overlooking central Taiz: Jabal Saber and its highest peak, Jabal al-Arus. The government says the Houthis want to seize this strategic peak”, she added.

The Houthis said there have been 105 air strikes and missile attacks by the Saudi-led coalition targeting civilian sites in Sanaa and 10 governorates on Wednesday.
